newsitem.title: USA: Study says HMOs often fail to diagnose skin cancer.
newsitem.headline: Study says HMOs often fail to diagnose skin cancer.

text.p: Health maintenance organisations are often ill-equipped to detect skin cancer because they require patients to see a primary care physician before going to a specialist, a new study has found.

Primary care physicians, who make the decision whether to refer a patient to a dermatologist, are often not adequately trained to diagnose skin cancer, according to the study, which was conducted by the University of California at San Francisco. Results are published in the September issue of the Archives of Dermatology.

"If managed care demands that primary care physicians be responsible for the initial evaluation of patients, patient care must not be compromised as a result," the study's author, Dr. Barbara Gerbert, said in a statement.

"Primary care physicians' ability to make correct initial evaluations of skin lesions ... determines whether or not patients with skin cancer receive the benefits of early detection and treatment," added Gerbert, who chairs the UCSF Division of Behavioural Sciences.
The study compared the diagnoses of 71 primary care residents to those of 15 dermatologists from seven different San Francisco-area hospitals.

The researchers found that primary care doctors failed 50 percent of the time to diagnose non-melanoma skin cancer and malignant melanomas correctly, compared with a failure rate of 17 percent among the dermatologists.
It also found that primary care physicians failed to recommend biopsies for cancerous lesions 33 percent of the time, while dermatologists failed to do so 19 percent of the time.

Regarding malignant melanoma alone, primary care doctors failed to diagnose that most deadly form of skin cancer 40 percent of the time, while the dermatologists failed to do so 26 percent of the time.
In addition, the primary care physicians had a higher rate of misdiagnosing benign lesions as cancer.

The HMO or managed care system, which is becoming increasingly prevalent in the United States, is based on controlling medical costs through preventative measures. Patients seeking care under this type of health insurance must first see a primary care physician, who decides whether a referral to a specialist is necessary.
